lessons.title: Preparing for a safe dissection
lessons.html:
Why dissect?

Dissection lets a student, extension officer or production manager see the real anatomy behind production problems: a fluke-damaged liver, pneumonia in a lamb's lungs, or the four compartments of a ruminant stomach. Dissections are usually done on animals already slaughtered or that died on the farm, under supervision of a lecturer or vet.

Choosing the specimen

  • Use material from a registered abattoir, a teaching specimen, or a farm animal whose death has been investigated by a vet.
  • Never open an animal that died suddenly with dark blood from the nose, mouth or anus. Anthrax is possible; call the state vet and leave the carcass unopened.
  • Animals suspected of rabies or other controlled diseases must be reported and handled only by officials.

Personal protective equipment and hygiene

  • Overall or apron, rubber boots, gloves (nitrile or rubber), and eye protection against splashes.
  • Cover cuts on your hands before you start.
  • Do not eat, drink or smoke in the dissection area.
  • Wash and disinfect hands, instruments and surfaces afterwards.

Instruments

InstrumentUse
Scalpel or skinning knifeSkin and tissue incisions
ForcepsHolding tissue
Scissors (blunt and sharp)Opening intestines and membranes
Bone saw or shearsOpening the rib cage or skull
Sharpening steelKeeping knives sharp; a blunt knife slips and causes injury

Always cut away from your body and away from other people. Keep the free hand behind the blade, and wear a cut-resistant glove on the non-knife hand where available.

lessons.title: Systematic dissection and recording
lessons.html:
Working in a fixed order

A systematic method ensures nothing is missed and findings can be compared. A common order for a ruminant such as a sheep is:

  1. External examination: body condition, eyes, mouth and teeth (age), skin, wool, hooves, udder or testes, external parasites.
  2. Positioning: lay the carcass on its left side so the rumen lies underneath and organs on the right are easy to reach.
  3. Skin and open: reflect the skin, then open the abdominal cavity carefully along the midline without puncturing the gut.
  4. Abdominal organs: note position, then examine liver (and bile ducts for fluke), spleen, kidneys, rumen, reticulum, omasum, abomasum and intestines.
  5. Thoracic organs: open the chest, examine the heart, lungs, trachea and lymph nodes.
  6. Head and other tissues as needed, for example the brain if nervous signs were seen.

What to record

Describe each organ by size, colour, texture, smell and any lesions. Use measurements and clear terms: 'liver enlarged, pale, bile ducts thickened with flat leaf-shaped parasites' is far more useful than 'liver bad'. Photographs help when the case is discussed with a vet.

Comparing species

A chicken dissection shows a crop, proventriculus and gizzard instead of a rumen; a pig shows a simple stomach and long intestines. Comparing species helps learners understand why rations and health programmes differ.

Sampling

If a disease is suspected, a vet may take samples for a laboratory. Samples must be labelled, kept cool as instructed and sent with a history of the case.

lessons.title: Disposal and interpreting findings
lessons.html:
After the dissection

Safe disposal

Carcass material can spread disease to people, dogs, jackals and other stock. Dispose of it promptly by an approved method such as a deep pit with lime covered well with soil, incineration, or collection by a licensed service. Never leave remains for dogs to eat, as this spreads tapeworm cysts and other diseases. Site any burial pit away from boreholes, rivers and dams to protect water, in line with the National Water Act 36 of 1998.

Cleaning up

  • Clean instruments in water and detergent, then disinfect and dry.
  • Wash down the table or slab and drain to an appropriate system.
  • Remove PPE carefully, gloves last, and wash hands thoroughly.
  • Seek medical help for any cut received during dissection and tell the doctor what you were handling.

Interpreting what you found

Link each finding back to management. Fluke-damaged livers point to wet camps or vlei areas and a need for a fluke control strategy. Many lung lesions in feedlot lambs suggest problems with ventilation, transport stress or vaccination. Thin animals with empty rumens in winter may indicate a feed gap. Write a short report: history, findings, likely cause and recommended action, and discuss it with your vet.

Key points

  • Never open an animal that may have died of anthrax; report it.
  • Wear PPE, cut away from yourself and keep knives sharp.
  • Follow a fixed order and record findings precisely.
  • Dispose of remains safely, away from water sources and dogs.
  • Use findings to improve herd management.
